passage: "Hafsa, the radio says the cyclone might reach the coast tonight. Help me fill the water buckets." "Noor Appi, they say that every year." Hafsa didn't look up from her phone. "Last time it was just rain." "This time the fishermen didn't go out. Ammi's already packed the documents." "Ammi packs the documents if a cloud looks at her." Hafsa scrolled past a video of waves. "Nothing ever happens on our street." "Then fill the buckets for nothing. Ten minutes." "After this video." Outside the window, the coconut palms were bending lower than Hafsa had ever seen. She glanced up once, then back at the screen. "Hafsa." "I heard you! It's fine. It's always fine." Noor dragged the buckets alone. The wind rattled the tin roof of the shed, and Hafsa turned the volume up.

qa.q: What had Ammi already done?
qa.a: Ammi had already packed the documents.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa feel so sure the cyclone won't matter?
qa.a: Past warnings ended in "just rain" and nothing ever happens on her street, so the ordinary past makes her feel safe tonight too.

qa.q: Which moment could have been Hafsa's turning point, and what could she have done then?
qa.a: When she saw the palms bending lower than ever. She could have put the phone down and helped fill the buckets, because the signs were different this time.

qa.q: What is it like for Noor to drag the buckets alone?
qa.a: Noor is worried and doing the work while Hafsa brushes off every warning, which could leave Noor frustrated as well as anxious.

passage: I'm Mridul, and I still think about that August evening. The district alert came as a text: the river was rising, and low areas should move valuables up and be ready to leave. Sumit messaged, "We're shifting to my uncle's place, you?" I sent back a laughing face. Our lane had never flooded in my whole life. I lay on the bed scrolling cricket clips while Baba stacked the rice sacks on the table, and I honestly felt calm, as if the alert was meant for some other town. At two in the morning the water came under the door. We carried the books and the gas cylinder upstairs in the dark, Baba shouting, my little sister crying. Nobody got hurt. But my schoolbag, left on the floor, was ruined. Now when an alert comes, I don't check my memory first. I check the alert.

qa.q: What did Sumit's message say?
qa.a: "We're shifting to my uncle's place, you?"

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel calm while Baba stacked the rice sacks?
qa.a: Mridul's lane had never flooded, so the alert felt meant for some other town rather than for their own home.

qa.q: What does Mridul now do differently when an alert comes, and why is that wiser?
qa.a: Mridul checks the alert instead of trusting memories of past years, because a lane that never flooded can still flood.

qa.q: How might Sumit have taken Mridul's laughing reply?
qa.a: Sumit, whose family was already leaving, may have felt uneasy or brushed off, seeing a friend treat a real warning as a joke.

passage: Note from Shalini, hostel warden, Friday evening. The cyclone alert came at 4 pm and we moved the girls to the ground-floor hall with torches and water. Kavitha, Class 9, stayed on her bed in Room 12, scrolling her phone. When I went up, she said, "Ma'am, this happens every monsoon. Nothing ever comes." She wasn't being rude; she looked genuinely relaxed, even amused at the fuss. The windows were already rattling. I sat on the next bed and said, "You may be right. But the alert isn't about last year. It's about tonight." She rolled her eyes, but she came down. At 9 pm a branch smashed the window of Room 12. Kavitha went very quiet when she saw the glass. Tomorrow I'll talk with her, not to scold, just to hear what she thinks now.

qa.q: What happened at 9 pm?
qa.a: A branch smashed the window of Room 12.

qa.q: What does Kavitha going very quiet at the sight of the glass suggest?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably shaken, realising that the danger she had shrugged off was real and had reached the very room where she had been lying. 😰

qa.q: What made Shalini's approach work in Room 12?
qa.a: Shalini did not argue or shame Kavitha. By granting that Kavitha might be right but pointing out the alert was about tonight, Shalini got her to come down.

qa.q: How might the other girls in the hall have seen Kavitha staying upstairs?
qa.a: They might have worried about her, or wondered whether they were overreacting, since one relaxed classmate can make a warning seem less serious.

grounding: A warden records how a teenage girl dismissed a cyclone alert as nothing new and kept scrolling until persuaded to move.

Thursday night

It's pouring right now. Like, loud. The TV says the local trains are slowing. I'm lying here scrolling reels and I honestly feel fine. Nothing ever actually happens to us.
Ritu

Monday. The TV in the hall said a cyclone was forming in the bay and might reach the coast by Thursday. Rajni, fifteen, glanced up from her phone. "It always turns away from us," she said, and went back to scrolling. Eshaan, her older brother, stayed watching the map.
Wednesday. School was shut. Rain hammered the tin roof next door. A loudspeaker van passed, telling families near the creek to move to the shelter at the government school. Rajni was on her bed with earphones in. "Nothing ever happens here. Relax," she messaged her friends.
Saturday. The family was back from two nights at the shelter. The coconut tree outside lay across their gate. Their kitchen wall was cracked. Rajni stood in the mud for a long time, her phone in her pocket.

qa.a: To the shelter at the government school.

passage:
Sit, Pallavi. You're scrolling while the radio talks about the river, and it reminds me of something.
When I was sixteen, in Guwahati, I had my first phone. The river was rising and the evening news said low areas should move to higher ground. Our lane had never flooded, not once. I lay on the charpai playing a silly game and told your Nani, my mother, "It's just the news making drama."
My friend Moni called at nine. Her family was leaving. I told her she was being dramatic too.
At midnight the water came under our door. We carried Nani's sewing machine up to the neighbour's roof in the dark. I remember my phone died up there, and I didn't even care.
So I'm your Sonali Masi, and I'm telling you: the river doesn't know what happened last year.

qa.q: What did Sonali and her family carry up to the neighbour's roof?
qa.a: They carried Nani's sewing machine up to the neighbour's roof.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she called the news "drama"?
qa.a: She felt safe and a bit dismissive, sure their lane would stay dry because it never had flooded before.

qa.q: When Moni called at nine, what could the young Sonali have done instead?
qa.a: She could have taken Moni's leaving as a sign to pack up and move with her family to higher ground before dark.

qa.q: How might Moni have felt when Sonali called her dramatic?
qa.a: Moni might have felt hurt and worried for Sonali, since her own family was taking the warning seriously.

The power had been out since four, and Damini's phone was at eighteen percent. Rain drummed so loudly on the roof of the hill-town house that she had to turn her videos up to full.
Her cousin Gopika texted: "Did you see the alert? River road families to shift to the school." Damini sent back a sleepy face. They lived right beside the river road, but the river had stayed in its bed every monsoon she could remember.
"Damini, pack a bag," her mother called from the dark.
"It never comes up this far, Mummy."
She kept scrolling. Twelve percent.
At seven the neighbour banged on their door with a torch. The water had crossed the road. Damini grabbed her charger, then realised there was no power to use it, and ran out holding her mother's hand.

The cyclone warning flashed on every news channel in Chennai: stay indoors, move vehicles to higher ground, keep supplies ready. Gopika lay on the sofa scrolling. "Amma, they say this every year. Nothing ever happens on our street."
Her mother, Bhavna, was already filling water bottles. "Last year was nothing. This one is different."
Gopika shrugged and went back to her videos. She had lived here all her life. The worst so far had been a wet school shoe.
By evening the wind was howling and water was creeping up the ground-floor steps. Bhavna called the building secretary, moved the family documents and Paati's medicines upstairs, and made Gopika carry the torch and the phone charger.

passage:
Looking back, I'm amazed how calm I was. I'm Tenzin, and last monsoon the district sent a landslide alert for our hillside in Sikkim. The hostel warden, Naveen sir, told us to pack a bag and be ready to move to the school hall. I didn't pack. I lay on my bunk scrolling, thinking: I've lived on this hill for sixteen years. The hill doesn't move.
At midnight a crack of stones woke us, and Naveen sir was calling names in the corridor with a torch. I went down in slippers, no bag. In the morning we saw a slide had covered the path behind the hostel. Nobody was hurt. But I still think about how normal everything felt, right up to the sound.

qa.q: Where were the students told to move?
qa.a: To the school hall.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while lying on the bunk?
qa.a: Tenzin felt calm and safe, sure the hill wouldn't move because it never had.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do differently at the next alert?
qa.a: Pack the bag at once and follow the warden's instructions, rather than trusting that ordinary days will continue.

qa.q: What might Naveen sir have felt at midnight?
qa.a: Naveen sir was likely frightened and focused, rushing to account for every student with a torch.

grounding: A teenager looks back on ignoring a landslide alert because the hillside had always been safe, while the warden acted to protect everyone.

passage:
Housemaster's note, St Mary's hostel, Puri, 18 October

The cyclone warning came over the radio at 4 pm: landfall expected within a day, move to the inland shelter. Most boys packed. I found Thomas in the common room, scrolling his phone, feet up. When I told him to pack, he said, 'Sir, every year they say cyclone. Nothing ever happens here.' Rehana, his classmate who is a day scholar, had come to collect her books; she said, 'My father says this one is different.' Thomas laughed. I stood beside him until he closed the phone and packed a bag, and we left on the 6 pm bus. By midnight the wind had taken the tin roof off the dining hall. I will talk with the whole house about warnings next week.

Rev. Paul, housemaster

qa.q: At what time did the warning come over the radio?
qa.a: At 4 pm.

qa.q: Why was Thomas scrolling with his feet up while others packed?
qa.a: Thomas felt relaxed and safe, sure nothing would happen because nothing bad had happened in earlier years.

qa.q: What did the housemaster do that made the difference?
qa.a: The housemaster stood beside Thomas until he packed and got him on the 6 pm bus, instead of just telling him once.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when Thomas laughed at her warning?
qa.a: Rehana may have felt worried and brushed off, since her father's warning was serious.

passage:
Saturday night, Guwahati

The flood warning came on the TV at dinner: the river rising, low areas to move to higher ground. Our colony is low. Mummy started packing. I stayed on the sofa watching videos. I told Saurabh on the phone, 'Every monsoon they say flood. It never reaches us.' He said his family was leaving for his Mama's place. I rolled my eyes. It felt like any Saturday. Then Papa switched off the Wi-Fi, stood in front of me and said, 'Bag. Now.' I packed, annoyed. We drove to Mausi's in the hills at ten. At midnight Saurabh sent a photo: water up to the second step of our building. My stomach went cold. I keep thinking: I really believed it couldn't happen because it hadn't before.

Naveen

qa.a: To Mausi's place in the hills.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel on seeing Saurabh's midnight photo?
qa.a: Naveen felt shocked and frightened, with a cold stomach, realising how wrong the 'never reaches us' feeling had been.

qa.q: What could Naveen do differently when the next warning comes?
qa.a: Naveen could treat the official warning as real and start packing straight away, instead of trusting that past years were safe.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when he switched off the Wi-Fi?
qa.a: Papa was probably worried and firm, determined to get the family moving before the water rose.

The paper boats for Kartik Purnima were drying on the verandah when the panchayat van rolled through the village near Puri, its loudspeaker crackling: a cyclone warning, move to the school shelter by evening. Pooja, lying on the charpai with her phone, didn't look up.
"Pooja, Maa says pack your books," her cousin Pranav called, already untying the goats.
"Every year they shout this," she said, thumbing past a dance clip. "Remember last Kartik? Two drops of rain."
Outside, the sky over the casuarina trees had turned the colour of wet cement, and the palms were bending. Pooja pulled her dupatta over her feet and kept scrolling. Nothing had ever happened here. Why would it now?
